term:A/B Testing.deep_dive: Two versions run simultaneously on split live traffic so their real-world performance can be compared statistically before committing to one. For AI deployment it doubles as a governance control: the incumbent keeps serving most users while the challenger proves itself on a controlled slice.
term:A/B Testing.exam_tip: Distinguish from shadow mode — in A/B testing both variants affect real users; in shadow mode the challenger's outputs affect no one.

term:AI Impact Assessment.deep_dive: The AI-specific look-before-you-leap: a structured evaluation of a system's potential effects on individuals, groups, organizations, and society — broader than a DPIA (not limited to personal data) and increasingly expected by frameworks (ISO 42001 requires one) and laws. Anatomy: describe the system, identify affected parties, rate severity and likelihood, mitigate, decide on residual risk, revisit.
term:AI Impact Assessment.exam_tip: AIIA covers social/ethical/legal impacts broadly; DPIA is the GDPR-mandated subset for personal-data risk — scope is the difference.

term:AI Partner.deep_dive: A third party in the AI value chain that collaborates in developing, supplying, or operating AI capability — cloud platforms, model vendors, data suppliers, integrators. Partner risk is third-party risk: their training data, security posture, and model changes become your exposure without your visibility.
term:AI Partner.exam_tip: Whatever the partner does, accountability to regulators and affected individuals stays with the organization deploying the system.

term:Adversarial Example.deep_dive: An input crafted to make a model fail — perturbations often imperceptible to humans (a sticker on a stop sign, pixel noise on an image) that flip the model's output. Their existence is why security testing for AI includes adversarial robustness, not just conventional penetration testing.
term:Adversarial Example.exam_tip: Adversarial examples attack the model at inference time; data poisoning attacks it at training time — the timing distinction is tested.

term:Algorithmic Bias.deep_dive: Systematic unfairness in algorithmic outputs — sourced from unrepresentative training data, historically biased labels, proxy features, or feedback loops, and manifesting as disparate performance or outcomes across groups. It is a sociotechnical problem: the algorithm faithfully amplifies what the data and design gave it.
term:Algorithmic Bias.exam_tip: Bias can enter at every stage (data, features, labels, deployment) — answers locating it only in 'bad data' are incomplete.

term:Audit.deep_dive: Systematic, independent, evidence-based examination against defined criteria — a framework, standard, regulation, or the organization's own policies. For AI: internal audits check the governance program, algorithmic audits probe specific properties (bias, robustness), and external certification audits (ISO 42001) provide third-party assurance.
term:Audit.exam_tip: Independence and defined criteria make an audit an audit — the builders reviewing their own system informally is monitoring, not audit.

term:Benchmarking.deep_dive: Evaluating a model against standardized datasets or tasks to compare performance across models or over time. The governance caveat is benchmark gaming and distribution mismatch: excellent benchmark scores prove little about behavior on your population — which is why ARIA-style realistic evaluation exists.
term:Benchmarking.exam_tip: 'It scored well on benchmarks' never substitutes for validation on the deployment population.

term:Bias (Systematic Deviation).deep_dive: The ISO-flavored definition: systematic deviation from a true value or fair outcome — encompassing statistical bias (estimation error), computational bias, and the human/social biases that data absorbs. NIST SP 1270 organizes it in three categories: systemic, computational/statistical, and human-cognitive.
term:Bias (Systematic Deviation).exam_tip: Bias is not only prejudice — statistical deviation counts too; the NIST three-category taxonomy is the tested structure.

term:Bias Testing.deep_dive: Empirically measuring model performance and outcomes across demographic slices — error rates, positive rates, and calibration per group, compared against fairness metrics chosen for the context. It requires access to (or sound inference of) sensitive attributes, which is why governed access beats attribute deletion.
term:Bias Testing.exam_tip: Bias testing compares subgroup performance — overall accuracy alone can hide a 10-point gap between groups.

term:Brittleness.deep_dive: AI's tendency to fail abruptly and completely when conditions deviate slightly from training experience — the opposite of the graceful degradation engineering aims for. Brittleness is why edge-case and robustness testing exist, and why confident model output in unfamiliar territory is a hazard.
term:Brittleness.exam_tip: Brittleness = catastrophic failure on small distribution shifts; robustness is its antonym and the design goal.

term:Business Context.deep_dive: The organizational reality an AI system serves: objectives, sector, risk appetite, regulatory exposure, and the workflows it lives inside. Context determines proportionality — identical models warrant different governance in ad targeting versus clinical triage — and grounding systems in defined business context is the first design-phase control.
term:Business Context.exam_tip: ISO 42001's 'context of the organization' clause institutionalizes this — governance is always calibrated to context, never one-size.

term:Business Objectives.deep_dive: The measurable outcomes an AI initiative exists to achieve — defined before development so success criteria, validation thresholds, and monitoring targets have something to anchor to. Objectives also bound scope: a system approved to reduce fraud losses was not approved to screen employees.
term:Business Objectives.exam_tip: Success criteria defined up front enable everything downstream — their absence is the root cause in many 'what went wrong' scenarios.

term:Classic AI.deep_dive: The symbolic, rule-based tradition — knowledge encoded as explicit rules and logic (expert systems, search, planning) rather than learned from data. Its governance virtue is transparency: the rules can be read. Its limitation — brittleness outside coded knowledge — is what machine learning displaced.
term:Classic AI.exam_tip: Symbolic/classic AI = hand-coded rules, explainable; connectionist/ML = learned patterns, opaque — a recurring contrast pair.

term:Concept Drift.deep_dive: The world changing under the model: the relationship between inputs and outputs shifts (fraud patterns evolve, consumer behavior changes), so a model trained on yesterday's relationship degrades even if input data looks the same. Detection needs outcome monitoring, and the remedy is retraining on current reality.
term:Concept Drift.exam_tip: Concept drift = input→output relationship changes; data drift = input distribution changes — the exam tests the distinction precisely.

term:Conformity Requirements.deep_dive: The substantive bar a high-risk system must clear: risk management system, data governance and quality, technical documentation (Annex IV), record-keeping/logging, transparency and instructions for use, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity. Conformity assessment verifies these; CE marking declares them.
term:Conformity Requirements.exam_tip: Learn the requirement set as a chain — exam questions ask which link is missing in a scenario.
